summary: Describes a mechanism for subscriber applications to request a continuous, customized stream of updates from a YANG datastore. This visibility into configuration and operational state changes allows remote mirroring and monitoring of devices.

plainLanguage.summary:
Network management apps usually work by asking a device for its state over and over. This RFC defines the opposite: an app asks to be told when the state changes, and the device streams the updates as they happen.

The app names the part of the device's data tree it cares about and says whether it wants a regular snapshot or a message each time something changes. Updates arrive as notifications, and the device applies the same access rules to pushed data as it would to a request.

questions: how to monitor yang datastore changes
what is a dampening period in yang push
subtitle: A subscription service that streams datastore changes to a monitoring application as they happen.

tldr.problem: Remote management still works by polling: the client asks for data on a timer. Polling is slow, easy to lose, hard to compare over time, and wasteful when the data rarely changes.
tldr.mechanism: YANG-Push lets a subscriber ask a device for a continuous stream of datastore updates. The subscription names the datastore, a filter that selects the data, and a trigger, either periodic or on-change, that decides when an update is produced.
tldr.outcome: Updates arrive as notifications rather than as replies to a request. The subscriber is told which subscription each update belongs to, and can tell a lost update from one that never existed, while access control on the pushed data matches a normal read.

facts.label: YANG Patch operations used
facts.value: create, delete, replace, insert and move

today: RFC 8641 is a Proposed Standard from September 2019 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It defines the datastore push part of the subscription framework whose transport and notification framework are set out in RFC 8639, and the document itself points to a separate specification for discovering which objects support on-change notifications.

sections.title: Why Polling Is Not Enough
sections.content:
Traditional ways of giving a remote system visibility into managed entities are built on polling, where a client periodically requests and retrieves data from a server to stay up to date. The RFC lists four problems with that approach.

Polling incurs significant latency, and that latency rules out many kinds of application. Polling cycles can be missed, and requests can be delayed or lost, often when the network is under stress and the need for the data is greatest. Polling requests can fluctuate slightly, producing intervals of different lengths, and the resulting data is hard to calibrate and compare. And for applications that monitor for changes, many remote polling cycles place unwanted and ultimately wasteful load on the network, the devices and the applications, particularly when changes happen only infrequently.

The alternative the RFC describes is for an application to receive automatic and continuous updates from a targeted subset of a datastore. That needs a service that lets applications subscribe to updates from a datastore and lets the server, the publisher, push and in effect stream those updates. The requirements for such a service were documented in RFC 7923.

This document defines the corresponding solution, built on top of RFC 8639. It supplements that work with YANG data model augmentations, extended RPCs and new datastore-specific update notifications. The transport options provided in RFC 8639 work seamlessly with the solution.
sections.plainLanguage: Polling is slow, can fail exactly when you need the data, and wastes effort on data that rarely changes. A subscription inverts it: the app registers its interest once and then receives the changes as they occur.

sections.title: The Vocabulary the RFC Introduces
sections.content:
The document reuses the terminology of RFC 7950, RFC 8341, RFC 8342 and RFC 8639, and adds terms of its own.

A datastore node is a node in the instantiated YANG data tree associated with a datastore, and is often called simply an object. A datastore node update is a data item holding the current value of a datastore node at the time the update was created, together with the path to that node. A datastore subtree is a datastore node and all its descendants.

A datastore subscription is a subscription to a stream of datastore node updates. There are two kinds. A periodic subscription is triggered according to some time interval. An on-change subscription is triggered when changes in the subscribed datastore nodes are detected.

A selection filter is evaluation or selection criteria applied against a targeted set of objects. An update record is a representation of one or more datastore node updates; it may also say what kind of change led to the update, whether the node was added, changed or deleted, and may carry other metadata such as the subscription identifier. Update records are often called simply updates. An update trigger is the mechanism that decides when an update record needs to be generated. YANG-Push is the subscription and push mechanism specified in the document.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC names the pieces of the service so that they can be referred to precisely: the objects on a device, the filter that picks which ones you want, the trigger that says when you get told, and the record that carries the news.

sections.title: The Subscription Model
sections.content:
YANG-Push subscriptions are defined using a YANG data model that enhances the subscription model of RFC 8639. The enhancements let subscribers say when update records are generated and what they contain.

The first enhancement is the specification of selection filters that identify the targeted YANG datastore nodes or subtrees for which updates are to be pushed. The second is the specification of update policies that contain the conditions that trigger the generation and pushing of new update records.

For a periodic subscription, the update trigger is two parameters: the period interval with which to report updates, and an anchor-time, a reference point in time that can be used to calculate at which points in time the periodic updates need to be assembled and sent.

For an on-change subscription, an update trigger occurs whenever a change in the subscribed information is detected. Three further parameters apply. The dampening period is the interval that has to pass before successive update records for the same subscription are generated for a receiver. It exists because detected changes should be sent as quickly as possible, but a rapid series of changes can exhaust resources in the publisher or the receiver. The dampening period applies to the whole set of datastore nodes selected by one subscription. When there is a change to one or more subscribed objects, an update record containing those objects is created immediately, or at the end of the dampening period if one is in effect. If several changes to a single object occur during a dampening period, only the value in effect when the record is created is included, and the period starts again each time the assembly of a record is completed.

The change-type parameter reduces the kinds of datastore change for which updates are sent, for example only sending an update when an object is created or deleted but not when a value changes. The sync-on-start parameter says whether a complete push-update of all subscribed data is sent at the beginning of a subscription. That early synchronisation establishes the frame of reference for the updates that follow.

The model also provides an encoding, using anydata, for the contents of periodic and on-change push updates.
sections.plainLanguage: A subscription has three parts. A filter picks the data you want. A trigger decides when you are told, either on a timer or when something changes. And a few extra knobs tune it, such as a waiting period that stops a flood of small changes from becoming a flood of messages.

sections.title: On-Change Subscriptions and the Dampening Period
sections.content:
On-change subscriptions let receivers get updates whenever changes to targeted objects occur. They are particularly effective for data that changes infrequently but that applications need to be told about quickly, with minimal delay, whenever a change does occur. They are also harder to implement than periodic ones, so not every implementation supports them, and not necessarily for every object.

Whether an on-change request is accepted when the scope contains objects that do not support on-change is up to the publisher. A publisher may accept such a subscription, in which case updates are sent only for the objects in scope that do support on-change, and the others are excluded from update records even if their values change. Objects are marked on the publisher so that a subscriber can tell which ones support on-change and which do not. Alternatively a publisher may simply reject the request, and for a configured subscription it may suspend it instead.

To avoid flooding receivers with repeated updates for fast-changing or oscillating objects, an on-change subscription can define a dampening period. Once an update record for a given object is generated, no other update for that subscription is created until the end of the period. The values sent at the end of the period are the values current at the end of the period for all changed objects, and changed objects include those deleted or newly created during the period. If an object returned to its original value, or was created and then deleted, during the period, that value is still sent, which shows that churn is occurring on the object.

The conceptual process for creating an update record is stated in five steps. Just before a change, or at the start of a dampening period, the filtering and access control rules are evaluated, giving a set A of datastore nodes and subtrees. Just after the change, or at the end of the dampening period, the rules are evaluated again, giving a set B. An update record is then constructed in the form of a YANG Patch record for going from A to B. If there were changes between A and B that cancelled each other out, the last change made is inserted into the patch even if the new value is no different from the original, because the interim changes cancelled out; a node created and then deleted is reported as a deletion, and a node deleted and then recreated is reported as a creation. If the resulting patch is not empty, it is sent to the receiver.

A subscriber that wants separate dampening periods for different objects can create several subscriptions with different selection filters.
sections.plainLanguage: When something changes, the publisher sends what changed rather than the whole picture. If a value keeps flapping, a waiting period holds the messages back and only the latest value is sent, with a note that the object was churning.

sections.title: How the Updates Are Streamed
sections.content:
Two generic YANG notifications carry the updates. A push-update defines a complete, filtered update of the datastore according to the terms of a subscription. It is used for continuous updates of periodic subscriptions. It must also be used as the initial push-update if the receiver has to be synchronised at the start of a new subscription, and it may be sent later if the publisher chooses to resynchronise an on-change subscription. The push-update record contains an instantiated datastore subtree with all the subscribed contents, and is equivalent to what the same data would give if retrieved explicitly with a datastore retrieval operation using the same transport and filters.

A push-change-update is the most common type of update for on-change subscriptions. Its record contains the set of changes that datastore nodes have undergone since the last notification message, so it says which nodes were created, which were deleted and which had their values changed. Where several changes occurred over a dampening period and the object was not deleted, the most current value is reported, so for each object only one change is reported rather than its whole history.

Both notifications are encoded and placed in notification messages, and are ultimately queued for egress over the specified transport. The RFC gives an example of a notification message for a subscription tracking the operational status of a single Ethernet interface, encoded in XML over NETCONF, and a second example for the on-change case, in which a YANG Patch replaces the operational status of the interface with the value down.

One detail of that example is the patch-id, whose value is 0. With YANG-Push, the publisher should put into the patch-id a counter starting at 0 that increments with every push-change-update generated for a subscription. If used as a counter, it must be reset to 0 whenever a resynchronisation occurs, that is, with the sending of a push-update, and it must be reset after passing the maximum value of 4294967295, the largest value the uint32 data type can hold. The mechanism makes it easy to identify lost or out-of-sequence update records.
sections.plainLanguage: Two kinds of message arrive. One carries the whole picture and is used on a timer. The other carries only what changed since the last message. Each change message is numbered, so a gap in the numbering tells the receiver that something was lost.

sections.title: The RPCs That Manage a Subscription
sections.content:
Subscriptions are established, modified and deleted with RPCs augmented from RFC 8639.

The establish-subscription RPC carries the parameters described in the subscription model. In the example in the RFC, the subscriber asks for the operational datastore, an XPath filter of /ex:foo, and a periodic subscription with a period of 500 centiseconds. A positive response includes the identifier of the accepted subscription. A request can be rejected for several reasons, including lack of authorization to establish a subscription, no capacity at the publisher, or the publisher being unable to select datastore content at the requested cadence. When the publisher cannot serve the request, it should include hints in the returned error that help the subscriber understand what parameters might have been accepted, carried in the yang-data structure establish-subscription-error-datastore. Even with the hints there is no guarantee that a later request will be accepted. The RFC also shows the error a publisher that can serve periodic updates but not on-change updates might return, with the reason on-change-unsupported.

The modify-subscription RPC carries the newly desired values for a subscription the subscriber established earlier. Parameters that are not included must remain unmodified. If the request is rejected, the existing subscription is left unchanged and the publisher must send an error response, which may again carry hints. A subscription may be modified many times. A configured subscription cannot be modified this way; its configuration has to be edited.

The delete-subscription RPC takes only the subscription identifier and is unmodified from RFC 8639. The resync-subscription RPC is supported only for on-change subscriptions that were established dynamically. On receipt, the publisher must either accept the request and quickly follow with a push-update, or send an error, which may carry a reason in the yang-data structure resync-subscription-error.

To make subscription requests at all, the subscriber needs to know the YANG datastore schemas the publisher uses. Those schemas are available in the YANG library module described in RFC 8525, and the receiver is expected to know the library information before starting a subscription. The set of modules, revisions, features and deviations can change at run time, and the YANG library provides a yang-library-change notification that tells the subscriber the library has changed, so that the subscription may need to be updated and the receiver may need to know about module changes in order to process updates correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: The subscriber drives everything with remote procedure calls: one to start a subscription, one to change it, one to stop it and one to ask for a fresh copy of everything. If the publisher cannot accept a request, it replies with a hint about what would have worked.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A receiver must only be sent updates that it is authorized to receive, and the publisher must ensure that no unauthorized data is included in push updates. To do so it has to apply all the checks that apply at the time of the update and, if necessary, silently remove any unauthorized data from datastore subtrees, which makes the authorization of pushed data equivalent to that of a regular get operation. Each push-update and push-change-update must have access control applied, and a publisher must silently omit data nodes the client is not authorized to see, following the conceptual authorization model of RFC 8341 extended to data nodes in notifications. A publisher must allow for the possibility that a subscription's selection filter references data that does not exist or that the receiver may not access, so that a receiver can monitor the whole lifecycle of a datastore tree without enumerating every node. If no objects remain in an update record after access control, a periodic subscription must still send an empty push-update, so that clients are not misled into thinking an update was lost, while an on-change subscription must not send one, so that clients remain unaware of changes to nodes they cannot read. If a receiver's read access is lost because of a permission change, that should be reported as a patch delete operation for on-change subscriptions; a publisher that cannot handle it that way must force the subscription to be re-established so that the right filtering is installed.

The YANG module defined in the document defines a schema for data designed to be accessed with network management protocols such as NETCONF or RESTCONF. The lowest NETCONF layer is the secure transport layer, and the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is Secure Shell. The lowest RESTCONF layer is HTTPS, and the mandatory-to-implement secure transport is TLS. The Network Configuration Access Control Model in RFC 8341 provides the means to restrict access for particular NETCONF or RESTCONF users to a preconfigured subset of the available operations and content. All the security considerations listed in RFC 8639 are also relevant for datastore subscriptions.

Several of the new data nodes are writable, and may be considered sensitive or vulnerable in some network environments. The subtree selection-filter under the container filters lets a subscriber say which objects or subtrees to include in a subscription. An attacker could try to modify the filter, for example so that very few objects are filtered in, to overwhelm the receiver, or so that certain objects are excluded, in which case certain changes would go unnoticed. The subtree datastore in the choice target in the list subscription has the same kind of risk, since changing the objects being filtered could overwhelm a receiver with a larger volume of updates than expected or cause changes to go unnoticed. The choice update-trigger in the list subscription is another: by modifying the update trigger an attacker might confuse a receiver, withhold updates, or overwhelm it, for instance by modifying the period of a periodic subscription or the dampening period of an on-change one, which either delays successive updates and affects the responsiveness of dependent applications, or produces a high volume of updates that exhausts receiver resources.

The access control model provides one means of mitigating these threats on the publisher side. To address them as a subscriber, the subscriber could monitor the subscription configuration for unexpected changes and subscribe to updates of the datastore nodes that represent its datastore subscriptions. As the volume of that data is small, a cautious subscriber could even fall back to occasional polling to guard against a compromised subscription.
sections.plainLanguage: The subscription itself is configuration, and configuration can be tampered with. A changed filter could flood the subscriber or hide changes from it; a changed timer could delay or overwhelm it. The subscriber is advised to watch its own subscription settings.

items.title: Selection filter
items.text: Which datastore nodes or subtrees the subscription covers. Either a subtree filter or an XPath expression.

items.text: For a periodic subscription, how often to report, and the reference point in time used to work out when.

items.title: Dampening period
items.text: For an on-change subscription, the interval that must pass before another update record is generated.

items.title: Change type
items.text: Which kinds of change to report, for example only creation and deletion.

items.title: Sync on start
items.text: Whether a full snapshot of the subscribed data is sent at the beginning.

items.desc: Used for newly created objects, except entries in a user-ordered list.

items.desc: Used for deleted objects, including entries in user-ordered lists.

items.desc: Used when only the object value changes.

items.desc: Used when a new entry is inserted into a list.

items.desc: Used when an existing entry in a user-ordered list is moved.

items.title: Transport security
items.text: NETCONF uses SSH and RESTCONF uses TLS, with access control from the Network Configuration Access Control Model.

items.title: A filter can be tampered with
items.text: An attacker could widen a selection filter to flood the receiver, or narrow it so that changes go unnoticed.

items.title: The trigger can be tampered with
items.text: Changing the period or the dampening period can delay updates, hide them, or overwhelm the receiver.

items.title: The subscriber can watch its own subscription
items.text: A subscriber can subscribe to updates of the datastore nodes holding its subscriptions, or even fall back to occasional polling.
